decisions.quote: The item-set response variability yielded mean crossmeasure correlations of r = .40 and .45 in T1 and T2, closely matching the preregistered expectation and conceptually replicating Baird et al. (2017). In contrast, the strict Baird-style reconstruction yielded considerably weaker mean correlations of r = .20 and .26. Given that the latter relied on substantially fewer responses within each variability component than Baird et al.’s original measures, these smaller associations should be interpreted in light of the reduced reliability expected from lower item counts.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly conclude that their preregistered analysis conceptually replicated Baird et al. (2017) and strongly supported their conclusion, attributing weaker correlations in the exploratory strict reconstruction to lower reliability from fewer items. The shipped quote from the abstract describes the extension to task engagement rather than a mixed replication verdict.

decisions.quote: Research Question 2 (RQ2) concerned how accurately established careless-responding indicators distinguish truthful from careless responding. The preregistered indicators were attention-check accuracy, fake-adjective accuracy, longstring, and page time. H2a: We predicted that all indicators would distinguish T1 and T2 from OC (H2a). H2b: For the covertly careless condition, we predicted substantially weaker discrimination than for overtly careless responding, with the possibility that some indicators might fail to distinguish truthful from covertly careless responding altogether.
decisions.reason: Inspecting the substantive relationship rather than section labels confirms that the paper does not re-test a specific empirical finding from Goldammer et al. (2020). In the Introduction (pp. 3–6), Goldammer et al. (2020) is cited alongside Curran (2016), Huang et al. (2012), and Meade and Craig (2012) as background on careless-responding indicators and the criterion problem, noting that repetitive-responding indicators like longstring (Johnson, 2005) do not necessarily distinguish careful from careless responders equally well. Rather than re-testing Goldammer et al.'s finding of weak longstring discrimination under induced carelessness, RQ2 tests a new adherence-monitored crossover design (truthful vs. overtly and covertly careless instructions) across attention checks, fake-adjective nonwords, longstring, page time, retest correspondence, and raw response variability, and H2a explicitly predicts the opposite of Goldammer et al.'s longstring result—namely, that all preregistered indicators (including longstring) would distinguish truthful from overtly careless responding. Only after H2a failed for longstring in the Results (p. 26) do the authors note post hoc in the Discussion (pp. 31–32) that their results were broadly consistent with Goldammer et al. (2020), while also contrasting their retest-correspondence measure with Goldammer et al.'s conventional personal-reliability indices and noting that their short item sequence provided only a limited test of longstring.

decisions.quote: The present study addressed two preregistered questions concerning response variability and careless responding. First, we aimed to conceptually replicate Baird et al.’s (2017) finding that individual differences in response variability generalize across substantively different measures. Second, we examined how accurately established careless-responding indicators distinguish truthful from overtly and covertly careless responding.
decisions.reason: The study explicitly identifies only Baird et al. (2017) as the replicated target (RQ1), while RQ2 is an extension evaluating careless-responding indicators under monitored adherence (predicting in H2a that all indicators, including longstring, would detect overt carelessness). Goldammer et al. (2020) is cited as background literature and for post-hoc discussion comparison, not as a target original finding re-tested by this study.
